extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Mill's enumerated fallacies and methodological cautions for evaluating scientific reasoning, observation, and induction. Useful for diagnosing reasoning errors and guiding empirical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences_in_nature_vs_received_distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice that the differences in nature must correspond to our received distinctions: effects we call by different names and arrange in different classes must be of different natures and have different causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against letting popular language and everyday phraseology determine scientific classification. Examples: Greek philosophers who studied meanings of words (Aristotle) and tried to deduce facts from these verbal distinctions; advice is to avoid mistaking linguistic classes for natural classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine_of_contrarieties
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of contrarieties: assuming adjectives or substances opposed in common language point to fundamental natural antitheses that must be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Pythagoreans extracting paired principles (Limited/Unlimited, Odd/Even, One/Many, etc.) and Aristotle deducing four elements by such oppositions. Anti-pattern: inferring ontological dualities solely from linguistic or conceptual contraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevating_language_relations_over_facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Making truth depend upon the relations of terms or the common use of language rather than on empirical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: treating the various senses of 'in' to decide if void exists. Mill (via Whewell) criticizes starting from 'we say thus' instead of observed phenomena. Remedy: prefer observation/experiment to verbal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective_analysis_of_notions_over_objective_observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The error of attempting to discover facts by analyzing common notions and abstract conceptions rather than by studying external facts themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes early Greek and medieval speculation; anti-pattern is treating philosophical inquiry as lexical or conceptual analysis rather than empirical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming_single_cause_(Baconian_oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's tacit assumption that a phenomenon has one invariable cause (forma) present in all cases; neglect of Plurality of Causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues this is false for most sensible qualities (heat, color, taste), which depend on many distinct causes. Practical implication: avoid searching for a single universal 'form' for a quality; consider multiple contributing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_effects_of_causes_over_causes_of_effects
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally more productive to inquire into the effects of a given cause (via experiment) than to attempt to infer the cause of a given effect directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that discovering causes is often achieved by first discovering effects of known causes; experiment is the efficient method for exploring effects. Anti-pattern: attempting to find cause solely by elimination on observed instances without experimental production of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes_must_resemble_effects_(a_priori_fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The a priori prejudice that the conditions or causes of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon itself (e.g., 'like produces like').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sympathetic magic, the 'Doctrine of Signatures' (turmeric for jaundice, fox lungs for asthma), and metaphysical theories (species sensibiles, ideas-as-images). Consequence: leads to fanciful hypotheses and misdirected remedies; avoid inferring causal likeness from superficial resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing_conditions_with_the_phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking of the conditions of a phenomenon as if they were the phenomenon itself (e.g., equating heat with a particular motion of particles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bacon’s 'forma calidi' presented as heat itself; Darwin's conflation of 'idea' with 'configuration of fibres'. Remedy: maintain clear distinction between an effect and the conditions or mechanisms that produce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: A_priori_theological_or_perfection_arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a priori notions of divine perfection or what ought to be (e.g., 'God is perfect; therefore nature must be perfect') to dismiss empirical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill criticizes arguments that reject observations because they would imply imperfection in God or a creator. Anti-pattern: letting metaphysical or theological intuitions override empirical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to observe facts or particulars that ought to have been observed; can be of instances or of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two forms: overlooking instances (failing to record contradictory cases) and overlooking circumstances (missing relevant contextual facts, e.g., collusion in fulfilled predictions). This leads to erroneous inferences and inadequate inductive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mal-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing something incorrectly—recognizing a fact wrongly and mistaking it for something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from mere omission; involves misperception or misinterpretation of observed phenomena. Example implications include misrecorded data or false identification of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective_memory_and_availability_bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When instances on one side of a question are more likely to be remembered and recorded than those on the other, producing a biased impression (e.g., credit kept for prophets despite many failures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes strong motives to remember successes and forget failures (fortune-tellers, almanac predictions). Consequence: persistence of false beliefs. Remedy: actively seek disconfirming instances and account for recording bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure_to_eliminate_chance_(Elimination_of_Chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting the requirement for a sufficient number of instances to rule out coincidences between unrelated events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill references the inductive notion of 'Elimination of Chance': a certain number of casual coincidences will occur, so one must gather enough instances to distinguish genuine causal connection from chance. Anti-pattern: attributing causation from few coincident instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating_insufficient_evidence_as_sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing the insufficiency of observed evidence with an adequate basis for induction; inferring general laws from inadequate samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill remarks this error overlaps with generalization fallacies; it often co-occurs with non-observation. Remedy: assess sufficiency of evidence before drawing general conclusions; distinguish errors due to evidence insufficiency from errors in inferential procedure.
